title: “DRAW ME AFTER YOU; LET US RUN”: The Woman in Scripture Who Wasn’t Ashamed to Express Desire
paragraphs: “DRAW ME AFTER YOU; LET US RUN”: The Woman in Scripture Who Wasn’t Ashamed to Express Desire

Song of Songs 1:4 is more daring than many Christians realize—and beneath its poetry is a truth about desire, intimacy, shame, and the God who does not redeem us by making us less human, but by making us holy.
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Read that again.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
Because it is almost startling that it is in the Bible.
A woman is speaking.
She is not emotionless. She is not embarrassed. She is not pretending she has no longing. She does not hide behind religious language or apologize for wanting to be near the man she loves.
She wants him.
She says it.
And Scripture does not censor her.
The Hebrew is even more vivid:
מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה
Māshkēnî ʾaḥăreykā nārûṣāh.
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Then comes the rest of the verse:
הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו
Hĕbîʾanî hammelekh ḥădārāyw.
“The king has brought me into his chambers.”
There it is.
Desire.
Longing.
Pursuit.
Intimacy.
Joy.
And not in some forbidden manuscript hidden from respectable Christians.
It is Holy Scripture.
Maybe that makes some of us uncomfortable.
And maybe our discomfort reveals something.
Because some Christians have unknowingly learned to treat holiness as though it means becoming less human.
We know how to talk about temptation.
We know how to warn people about lust.
We know how to say, “Flee sexual immorality.”
And Scripture absolutely does.
But sometimes we have been far less comfortable saying something else Scripture also says:
God created human beings capable of desire.
And desire itself is not the enemy.
Sin corrupts desire.
Sin disorders desire.
Sin can turn another human being into an object, turn affection into possession, turn longing into lust, and turn intimacy into exploitation.
But Christianity does not teach that the human body is evil.
It teaches something infinitely more beautiful.
The body belongs to God.
Love belongs to God.
Marriage belongs to God.
Faithfulness belongs to God.
And even our desires must ultimately come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because Song of Songs 1:4 is not a frightened woman trying to erase her femininity.
She speaks.
She longs.
She desires closeness.
And the biblical text lets her voice remain.
The Hebrew verb behind “draw me” is מָשַׁךְ — māshakh.
It can carry the sense of drawing, pulling, or leading.
In this verse the form מָשְׁכֵנִי — māshkēnî — is intensely personal:
“Draw me.”
Then suddenly her language expands:
נָּרוּצָה — nārûṣāh.
“Let us run.”
There is movement in this love.
Not indifference.
Not coldness.
Not detached admiration from a safe distance.
Run.
The woman of the Song does not merely want to analyze love.
She wants to experience the presence of the one she loves.
And perhaps that is where this ancient love song begins exposing something much deeper in us.
Because we are creatures of desire.
Every one of us is running after something.
Some run after affection.
Some run after validation.
Some run after money because poverty once terrified them.
Some run after applause because silence makes them feel invisible.
Some run from relationship to relationship because being wanted for one night feels temporarily better than feeling unwanted for a lifetime.
Some scroll through photographs hoping someone else's life will distract them from their own loneliness.
Some keep returning to pornography because counterfeit intimacy seems easier than vulnerability.
Some stay in destructive relationships because crumbs of affection feel better than an empty table.
Some pretend they do not need anyone.
Some hide behind ministry.
Some hide behind marriage.
Some hide behind jokes.
Some even hide behind theology.
But eventually, when the room becomes quiet enough, the heart asks the question we have been avoiding:
What am I really longing for?
That is where Song of Songs becomes dangerous in the best possible way.
It refuses to pretend desire does not exist.
The woman does not say, “I have transcended longing.”
She essentially says:
Draw me.
I want to come closer.
And Scripture is not ashamed of her.
But we must also be careful here.

Song of Songs is poetry celebrating human love and desire. We should not erase its plain literary meaning by pretending every kiss, fragrance, chamber, or embrace is secretly a coded reference to Christ.
The lovers are lovers.
The poetry is romantic.
The desire is real.
And that is part of its biblical beauty.
Yet when the whole canon of Scripture is opened before us, this celebration of rightly ordered human longing can also become a mirror.
Not because the woman in Song 1:4 is secretly saying the name of Jesus.
She isn't.
But because every good created love ultimately reminds Christians that no created person can carry the full weight of the human soul.
Your husband cannot be your Savior.
Your wife cannot be your Savior.
Your boyfriend cannot be your Savior.
Your girlfriend cannot be your Savior.
Sex cannot save you.
Marriage cannot save you.
Being desired cannot save you.
Being beautiful cannot save you.
Being wanted cannot save you.
And being alone cannot condemn you.
There is a hunger underneath all our hungers that creation was never designed to satisfy completely.
We were made for God.
And this is where the words begin to sound different in the heart of a Christian:
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Because Jesus Christ does not merely tell sinners to find their way home.
He comes looking for them.
Think about the scandal of the Gospel.
God did not wait until you became desirable.
Christ did not die for a polished version of you.
He did not climb Calvary for the person you pretend to be on Sunday.
He knew.
The secret browser history.
The affair nobody discovered.
The fantasies.
The jealousy.
The hunger for attention.
The compromises.
The relationship you knew was pulling you away from God.
The nights you promised, “Never again,” only to fall again.
The shame beneath the smile.
The prayer life that disappeared.
The Bible collecting dust while your phone knew exactly what could keep you awake until 2:00 in the morning.
He knew.
And still—
the cross.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God taking sin so seriously that the Son of God bears judgment so sinners can be reconciled to Him.
Jesus does not simply validate every desire we possess.
Some desires must die.
Some must be disciplined.
Some must be redirected.
Some must be confessed.
Some must be surrendered.
Jesus loves us too deeply to call our chains freedom.
But He also loves us too deeply to leave repentant sinners chained to their shame.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide because if anyone knew you, they would leave.”
The Gospel says something stronger:
God already knows.
Now come home.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You have spent years trying to become impossible to reject.
You changed your body.
Changed your personality.
Lowered your standards.
Ignored warning signs.
Stayed when you should have left.
Gave pieces of yourself away because you thought love had to be purchased with access to you.
Maybe somebody told you that if you really loved them, you would cross a boundary your conscience was begging you not to cross.
Maybe you confused being desired with being cherished.
And afterward, when everything collapsed, you blamed yourself.
So now words like purity make you uncomfortable.
Words like intimacy make you afraid.
And words like desire make you ashamed.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make ashamed people behave better.
He came to redeem sinners.
He came to forgive.
To cleanse.
To restore.
To make new.
The Gospel is not God shouting from heaven, “Clean yourself before you approach Me.”
It is Christ entering our ruin and saying, in effect, “Follow Me.”
And that changes everything.
Because biblical repentance is not merely running from sin.
It is running to Someone.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers others avoided.
The One who received broken people religious society had already categorized.
The One who looked at sinners without becoming casual about their sin.
The One who could say both, “Neither do I condemn you,” and, “Go, and sin no more.”
Grace and truth.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Welcome and repentance.
The Gospel refuses to separate what we keep trying to tear apart.

And suddenly those ancient words become a prayer worth borrowing—not as though Song of Songs 1:4 were originally written as a direct prophecy about Christ, but as language that beautifully expresses the surrendered longing of a redeemed heart:
Draw me, Jesus.
Because left to myself, I keep running toward things that cannot save me.
Draw me when temptation looks beautiful.
Draw me when loneliness starts negotiating with my convictions.
Draw me when old messages appear on my phone.
Draw me when I miss someone You delivered me from.
Draw me when pornography promises comfort.
Draw me when bitterness feels justified.
Draw me when applause becomes addictive.
Draw me when success starts becoming my god.
Draw me when religion becomes easier than relationship with You.
Draw me when I am tired.
Draw me when I am ashamed.
Draw me when I have fallen again.
Draw me after You.
And let me run.
Not crawl toward Christ while constantly looking backward at Egypt.
Run.
Run toward mercy.
Run toward truth.
Run toward the Word.
Run toward prayer.
Run toward repentance.
Run toward the wounded hands that already know exactly what you have done.
This is what makes Christianity so radically different from self-improvement.
Jesus is not offering you a slightly cleaner version of your old life.
He calls you to die and live again.
The scandal becomes testimony.
The addict becomes free.
The adulterer can become faithful.
The liar can become truthful.
The bitter can forgive.
The sexually broken can learn holiness.
The ashamed can lift their head.
Not because sin suddenly becomes insignificant.
Because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
That is the heart of From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal celebrated.
Scandal redeemed.
Not sin renamed.
Sin forgiven.
Not brokenness romanticized.
Brokenness brought to Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite your past by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites what your past gets to mean.
The wound does not have to become your identity.
The failure does not get the final sentence.
The person who abandoned you does not get authorship over the rest of your life.
The sin you confessed does not outrank the blood Christ shed.
Your worst chapter is not sovereign.
Jesus is.
And maybe right now you finally understand why the woman saying “Draw me” matters.
There is no shame in wanting.
The question is what your wanting is teaching you to worship.
There is no holiness in pretending you have no desires.
Holiness means bringing those desires under the authority of the One who created you.
Maybe you desire marriage.
Tell God.
Maybe you ache for affection.
Tell Him.
Maybe you are sexually frustrated.
Tell Him.
Maybe you are lonely enough that obedience sometimes physically hurts.
Tell Him that too.
God is not intimidated by honesty.
He already knows what is happening inside you.
Prayer is not informing God.
Prayer is opening the locked rooms.
And some of us have spent years inviting Jesus into the living room while keeping Him out of the bedroom.
Out of our relationships.
Out of our fantasies.
Out of our private messages.
Out of our browser.
Out of our loneliness.
Out of the parts of ourselves we decided were too embarrassing to bring before God.
But there is no discipleship without surrender.
You cannot say, “Draw me after You,” while continually planting your feet against Him.
There comes a moment when grace demands a response.
Delete the number.
End the secret relationship.
Confess the lie.
Ask for help.
Put accountability around the addiction.
Forgive the person.
Stop feeding what you keep asking God to kill.
Come into the light.
And run.
Be honest.

And if God has already carried you out of something you thought would own you forever, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs to survive tonight.
Send this privately to the person who has been ashamed to come back to God.
There is also another way to stand with this work.
Scripture does not give us the right to say that.
Paul wrote that giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
That matters.
Giving should be worship, not manipulation.
So pray.
Honor your responsibilities.
Support your local church and faithful Gospel work as the Lord leads you.
Financial support is not the only way to help, either.
Every share can become a doorway.
Every tag can become an invitation.
Every sincere comment can tell another struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
But merchandise is not the reason to stay close.
Jesus is.
Come to Christ.
Not when you become less broken.
Now.
Not after you defeat every temptation.
Now.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
You will never purchase grace with worthiness.
Come because Jesus died for sinners.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because forgiveness is real.
Come because repentance is possible.
Come because the same Gospel that exposes sin also announces mercy.
Come because you were never meant to spend your entire life running after things that keep leaving you empty.
The woman in the Song cried:
מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה
“Draw me after you; let us run.”
Thousands of years later, perhaps those words can become the cry of your surrendered heart.
Jesus...
I have run after enough things.
I have chased people.
Pleasure.
Approval.
Attention.
Success.
Desire.
Comfort.
I have exhausted myself trying to drink from cups that never stayed full.
So draw me.
Draw the parts of me still resisting You.
Draw the wounded parts.
Draw the ashamed parts.
Draw the desires I do not know how to control.
Draw the memories I cannot erase.
Draw the heart that keeps wandering.
Draw me after You.
And this time...
let me run.
Because perhaps the most dangerous distance in your life was never how far you wandered.
It was believing that after everything you had done, Jesus would no longer call you home.
